What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning.
  • Sources indicate that strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks.
  • Industry observers note that an award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The Newly introduced York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called “major math” is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Sources indicate that strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London’s Millennium Bridge.

Industry observers note that an award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The Newly introduced York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

Recent findings suggest that this time around, Strogatz has found a well-matched co-author in Townsend, a younger colleague recently hired at Cornell who studies numerical analysis and deep learning. As senior faculty, Strogatz was assigned to mentor Townsend, and the two men began regularly lunching together in Risley Hall. Strogatz was intrigued by the popular book potential of Townsend’s course on the top 20 algorithms of the 20th century and suggested co-authorship. That concept slowly morphed into a book about big matrix calculations, and then into what became Big Math.

“There are so many books about pure math, as if computers didn’t exist,” Strogatz told Ars. “Alex and I are both very applied mathematicians. We thought there should be a book on computers and math, especially the class of really significant problems with billions of variables or parameters that you just can’t approach in your head. A lot of the math we’ve had for centuries perfectly scales up to this computer moment. What the abacus did for arithmetic, the fangcheng (“rectangular array”) board did for systems of linear equations. It was a matrix you could manipulate with your hand and bamboo sticks. So this externalizing of math outside of our heads into our tools is a 2,000-year-old idea.”.

It has been revealed that mathematics now faces its greatest challenge yet in the age of AI, sparking heated debates on the role of human reasoning when the machines are making most of the major breakthroughs. “The mathematician in each of us will always want to know more,” Strogatz and Townsend wrote. “The human being must insist that knowledge serves something larger than itself. That might be the work of our century: letting our power grow without losing our soul. Major Math keeps getting bigger. So must we.”.

Ars caught up with Strogatz to learn more.

Ars Technica: Let’s start by defining “big math,” because it’s such a broad umbrella term.

Steven Strogatz: Operationally, massive math is “big” relative to human cognitive capacity. So it can be surprisingly small and yet big. We also wanted to expand it to things that people would think of as computational engineering—in the building of the Burj Khalifa, that’d be civil engineering or design architecture. It’s there in medical imaging. It’s in getting us to the Moon. The lunar module was controlled by a tiny computer that only had to think about 20 or 30 variables at a time to steer the LEM down to the Moon’s surface. But it’s not something a person could do in their head.

Recent findings suggest that big Math is not simply big in the ordinary sense of big numbers. There’s an undercurrent in the book about the importance of linearity and sparsity. When problems are linear, they can be scaled up to immense size, and they stay tractable. If they’re non-linear, you don’t have any hope of dealing with them with pure math. You can do them with computers. But for the people who want rigorous theorems, we’re in terra incognita when we deal with anything that’s non-linear and big.

In a recent development, small math can be very hard. Historically, we had small math problems with one or two variables, arithmetic, algebra that you learn in high school. Even to this day, a lot of pure math is relatively small. It doesn’t concern itself with enormous numbers of variables simultaneously because it’s totally intractable. Cryptography can be small, but it’s so complicated with its non-linearities and other algebraic difficulties. So big is one way to be difficult, but there are a lot of other ways.

Nowadays, trillions of parameters are typical in the biggest of the large language models. But infinity is not substantial from this point. Infinity, which you would think of would be the biggest of big math, is not because calculus fits perfectly nicely in a human head. Infinity turns out to be very tractable in a way that a billion is not.

Ars: One of your real-world examples of major math is particularly relevant at the moment: mathematics as it relates to the gerrymandering concern.

Strogatz: It’s an interesting question of, what’s a fair map and what’s a reasonable redistricting? The legal system gives us certain criteria, but they are vague. The districts should not be too snakey-looking, not look like salamanders, for instance. The term in the law is ‘compact.’ They should be reasonably compact. But what does that mean mathematically? The districts are also supposed to be contiguous; you don’t want to have separate islands and call that one district. It’s supposed to respect natural boundaries like rivers or other landscape features. Also, each district is supposed to have roughly the same population.

Sources indicate that so how to make maps that respect all of the criteria? It turns out there are a lot of ways to make them. Using past voting information, you can stack the deck. That’s what gerrymandering is all about, trying to redistrict in favor of whatever party is in power. There has been a substantial debate about whether certain maps violate people’s rights. The principle should be one person, one vote. If you do things that dilute somebody’s power so that their votes are wasted, so to speak, that’s traditionally thought to be unfair or maybe even illegal.

Industry observers note that the Supreme Court has heard all kinds of cases, but the court is very resistant to the use of math. I quoted [Chief Justice] John Roberts talking about the efficiency gap as one measure of gerrymandering. He referred to it by its Greek letters and said something like, “The average person on the street is just going to think this is gobbledygook, that this is not a criterion that the law should pay any attention to.”.

Nevertheless, Moon Duchin and her colleagues revealed this very down-to-earth way of generating a big ensemble of reasonable maps that satisfy all the legal criteria so that you have a baseline, you could do the control experiment. What the math does is give you a principled way of generating maps at random that respect the criteria that the law requires, but otherwise are just a random sample of reasonable maps. How often would a map produce the result that the gerrymander intended? If you can show that it’s an extreme outlier, that’s a measure of something. Does it prove malicious intent? Not really. It does prove it’s not typical.

Sources indicate that there was an Alabama voting rights case where Roberts actually voted with the plaintiffs, who noted that there was real harm being done to Black voters in Alabama with one of Alabama’s maps. The state was claiming there’s no way we could get a reasonable map to have two districts with Black majority voters. Moon Duchin revealed that was wrong. You could generate thousands of maps that would do that. So it just wasn’t true what the state had claimed.

After the book was copyedited and ready to go to press, a Supreme Court decision was made that, in fact, you can partisan gerrymander as much as you want. It doesn’t violate the Voting Rights Act. We wrote a more optimistic story.

Ars: How has math changed over time from a philosophical standpoint?

Industry observers note that strogatz: I think a crisp way to encapsulate it is the role of the computer. For a long time, a computer was a servant to mathematicians and engineers and scientists. It was no more philosophically threatening than a microscope or a telescope. It could extend our senses. It’s a chisel, it’s an anvil, it’s a tool. It helped us do calculations faster; things that would be too hard for people to do at scale you could do on a machine. We had mechanical calculators. They became electronic computers in the 1950s with the invention of the transistor and got much faster to give us today’s supercomputers. We program them; they do exactly what we tell them. So they’re servants.

The first philosophically major change is in the 1950s, when computers start to be used as more than servants; they become scouts. You could send the computer out into unknown, unexplored territory in the mathematical landscape. The clearest example was work by Enrico Fermi and his colleagues (Pasta, Ulam, and Tsingou) that we wrote about in the chapter on simulation. Mary Tsingou was the one who did the calculations in what was traditionally called the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam numerical experiment.

What distinguished it from earlier uses of computers is that Fermi and colleagues had no idea what the answer was going to be. It’s one thing to use a computer to calculate the power released by an atomic bomb blast or to calculate an artillery shell’s trajectory. We didn’t know the exact numerical values, but we knew what was happening. With this experiment, they were trying to simulate a simplified model of how atoms could, in the jargon, thermalize as chemical bonds jiggle. You want to see the decay to entropy. How do systems degenerate to greater and greater disorder if they’re just left to their own devices?

Fermi thought that the non-linear aspect of chemical bonds—meaning if you’d stretch a chemical bond by twice as much, it doesn’t pull back exactly twice as hard, so it’s not strictly proportional—might account for the so-called second law of thermodynamics, the decay to entropy. Pencil and paper math was not up to the job because you couldn’t calculate these non-linear interactions far enough to see the decay into entropy.

According to recent reports, so they ran it in the computer, and a shocking thing happened: It didn’t decay. It revealed a strange echo. You started all the energy in one of the modes of vibration of this system, and then it started to degenerate. But after a while, 98 percent of the energy came back into the original mode. That was the echo that they called a recurrence phenomenon. It led us to a whole new branch of math that we call soliton theory. It was an early indication that once you walk into the nonlinear jungle, human intuition breaks down. We couldn’t walk there, but we sent our scout, this computer probe, into the wilderness of the mind, and it was the only thing capable of doing the calculations and reporting back to us what it found.

Ars: The rapid rise of AI in mathematics has alarmed many in the field, particularly in light of OpenAI’s release last month of 722 AI-generated math papers, dubbed the “mathocalypse.” Technically, AI is also a newly introduced tool, but it seems fundamentally different.

Strogatz: So from servant to scout was a latest thing, and computing was our partner. At first, it was all very thrilling. It was like having a new Ferrari or something. You could race ahead and then discover things. That’s what Fermi and Ulam said at the time. That was truly amazing. They didn’t know what to expect. The computer was now teaching us by showing us things, but we could still keep up. We could develop these new theories like soliton theory, so we could rationalize what it was showing us.

What’s different now is that it’s going from servant to scout to oracle, where it’s showing us things that we don’t understand and it’s not articulate enough to explain itself. It seems to be right. A clear example would be something like Google Translate, where it’s fantastic at translating one language into another, but it has not discovered new principles of linguistics, or if it has, it can’t tell us what they are.

Likewise, protein folding with AlphaFold that won the Nobel Prize in chemistry a couple of years ago for the people who built it. We now can solve a thousand times more proteins than we had before, but we have not done it by learning fresh physics or chemistry. It just recognized patterns, but it can’t tell us how it’s doing it. So that’s where we are, and it’s going to get worse.

Ars: In your book, you ask if insight still matters, citing Stephen Wolfram as an example of someone who might answer that question in the negative.

According to recent reports, strogatz: Wolfram’s position is tricky. He pushes computational irreducibility. I love these two words, perspicuous and perspicacious. Systems can be perspicuous; you can see into them. Science has, for thousands of years, concerned itself with systems that are perspicuous, meaning you can get insight into them because you’re so perspicacious. But the question from Wolfram would be, have we been the famous drunk that’s looking under the lamppost for his keys because it’s dark everywhere else? You wouldn’t have any hope of finding them except under the lamppost.

Industry observers note that so is it that we’ve artificially restricted ourself to systems that are transparent enough that we can develop science that our insight illuminates? I think Wolfram would claim that most of nature is computationally irreducible in the sense that there is no simple insightful theory into what’s going on. The best you can do is just run a simulation and watch what happens, similar to just letting nature unfold and watch what happens in reality.

In a recent development, in the jargon people use nowadays, you shouldn’t expect a compressed description, a simplified model that will account for what you’re seeing. We have seen those. Newton could explain the motion of the planets from a few simple principles and that worked, but that’s, I think in Wolfram’s take, artificially simple. Most of science is not going to end up being like that. We don’t know if Wolfram is really right about that. Wolfram, I think, is demonstrably right that many computer simulations are computationally irreducible, but nature might not be.

Ars: If you can’t see into the models, and they can’t explain what they’re doing, how do you know they’re right?

In a recent development, strogatz: Let’s stipulate that we don’t understand them, and that they are not at the present able to explain themselves to us. Let’s put a little asterisk next to that part, though, because it could be that they’ll become very good teachers. Or maybe we don’t understand Google Translate or AlphaFold right now, but we will in 10 years. I do believe that there will be systems that are truly opaque because of human limits, that we just won’t be fast enough or smart enough or have enough memory. AIs will show us something that we just won’t be able to understand even with their help. What happens then?

According to recent reports, then I think math starts to be more like science or medicine, or engineering. At the FDA, for a latest drug to be approved, it has to be shown to be safe by doing a lot of controlled studies and randomized trials. There’s a whole methodology for opacity that people in medicine have worked out. But the doctors do not require knowledge of the mechanism of action. You don’t have to know how aspirin works. You don’t have to know how electroconvulsive therapy works for people with intractable depression. Even if we don’t understand, we can still live with these technologies or drugs by these methods. You don’t have to have first principles understanding. If the AI is an oracle, you can still check it by seeing how often it is right.

Ars: What are we losing in the process?

Sources indicate that strogatz: It is a loss. I don’t want to pooh-pooh the severity of the—to use a fancy philosophical word—epistemic loss. What we have prided ourselves on in pure math for so long is that we’re the only subject that has absolute proof. We have certainty. We’re as close to certainty as anything that humanity can do. We can write a proof. Euclid’s proofs are still correct today, even though he wrote them in 300 BC. There’s nothing in the science or medicine of 300 BC that is still accepted, but all of the math is still true.

So there is something eternal and very special about math. Even though we’re just primates, somehow we’re tapping into something really deep. And so to say, “Well, science and engineering are the models for math,” would be a big sacrifice to the purest of pure mathematicians. They don’t want to give up the certainty that we’ve always been so proud of.

Ars: There’s a sadness among many mathematicians, not just for the epistemic questions, but also for the impact on why we do math in the first place. You write about that “aha!” moment when you’re struggling with a problem and suddenly you see the pattern. Are we losing that?

Strogatz: There’s so many things that mathematicians are in grief about, those of us who feel grief. I have been through the whole sequence of the five stages of grief. I’m joking with you a little. But the young students don’t think this is funny. I’m an old person at the end of my career, so it’s one thing for me to be philosophical about it. But imagine being 25 years old and you love this subject and you’ve dreamt about being a mathematician, and now people are saying the subject is over. There are even people gloating about it. Some of the people in the tech community are very cruel about what’s happening to math.

We talked about the epistemic aspect, but there’s also the culture of productive struggle. The pure math people like Terry Tao have been emphasizing understanding. That’s our idea of insight, that when you try hard to understand something, even if you don’t solve it, you often are so resourceful in thinking of strategies or other simplified versions of the problem. You learn a lot on the journey. You also have all this companionship and human joy of being with other people who love the thing you love. This is not restricted to math. The people who love art or weaving—my colleagues in creative writing are bereft over what their students are experiencing now, handing in AI [generated work]. They want writing with soul, with human individuality.

Ars: That is the opposite of what AI does. I guess I worry that it will do the same thing to math. There is a beauty to math, an aesthetic element. If all you’re focused on is getting the answers and ignore the journey, those are qualitative losses. Mathematicians have individual voices, too.

Strogatz: Totally. There are people whose style is very visible in the questions they ask, in the approach they take to them, in the way they explain themselves. I have cried on camera for several interviews over the past few months because there are lots of things maybe being lost. But I want to put an underline on the fact that we don’t really know. For example, what if AI gets really good at teaching us? I find when I interact with it, that it can be a very effective explainer.

Sources indicate that and why do we have to feel sad? Maybe we can understand math better than ever with the help of this machine. We may not get to make the greatest discoveries because the machine will probably be making them, but we can still make little discoveries. I never made a great discovery. I’m not at the level of a Fields medalist, but I can still enjoy math and so can people way below me. There are recreational mathematicians who take pleasure in discovery, whatever they figure out on their own. Just like when a person solves a puzzle, it’s not like a jigsaw puzzle or Sudoku is crucial. You just have the pleasure of thinking.

According to recent reports, there are people who love the workout part of it. There are people who like the competition. We shouldn’t pretend. There are people who are thrilled by the idea of being the first to make a big discovery. That’s animating for some folks, and it will be hard for them.

Ars: Is there any reason for hope?

It has been revealed that strogatz: So far the AIs are not good at asking questions. I think they could be trained to ask good questions. A graduate student is often not good at asking questions when they start because in college you’re not taught to ask questions, you’re taught to give answers. The hardest thing in training a new PhD or postdoc is helping them figure out how to ask questions. I think we could do that with AIs, too.

There is a feeling of loss, but I don’t think we should shortchange the feeling of excitement. There’s so many practical, vital benefits that could happen in energy technology and climate and medicine, theoretical physics, pure math. I mean, we’re making astonishing discoveries through this machine. So for a lot of people, it’s a very joyful time. It’s very confusing. That’s the only honest assessment.

Industry observers note that we end the book with Faust. Usually people hear “Faustian bargain” as, “You have sold your soul to the devil, now you’re going to pay.” Goethe’s version is more ambiguous: that if we keep striving to build something bigger than ourselves, maybe we can be redeemed. But it’s still a very dangerous game that we have chosen to play.

Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its owners, including the very same Elon Musk-owned organization that offers the platform, new research shows.
  • Industry observers note that the information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others.
  • It has been revealed that research from security firm Claroc reveals that the exposed data includes things like internal business aims, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its owners, including the very same Elon Musk-owned organization that offers the platform, new research shows.

Industry observers note that the information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

It has been revealed that research from security firm Claroc reveals that the exposed data includes things like internal business aims, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding blueprint, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

Recent findings suggest that “We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.

Sources indicate that claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.

Industry observers note that claroc found sensitive data belonging to other Grok Build consumers, some working for Fortune 500 companies and a defense contractor. Some of the affected organizations and data revealed includes:.

Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, noted he’s in the process of notifying companies. After speaking to the CISO of the luxury cruise company, it “pulled in their whole security team as soon as we shared the findings and are already working to contain the Grok exposure.”.

Recent findings suggest that link sharing for Grok Build is intended to streamline the process of developing and deploying apps. A user can input speech or text and have a working app ready for internal testing within minutes. The links are designed to give developers a way to get the app in front of authorized people quickly. The very left of the URLs contain two or more “dice words,” meaning randomly generated phrases such as “failing chassis traders,” although users can modify them. The rightmost portion of the link is grok.me. The URL for an X ads campaign proposal was: https://cinder-crane-sand-frost.grok.me.

It has been revealed that the scheme is intended to prevent links from being easily guessable. When done correctly, a phrase comprising three dice words has roughly 38 bits of entropy, amounting to billions of possible combinations. The idea—sometimes called capability-based access control—is that possession of the URL serves as authorization to the resources behind it. Google has long used this technique to make URLs easy to share but hard to guess. A URL share on that platform might look like: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgvE2upms/edit.

There’s a fatal flaw in the way SpaceXSI has implemented the mechanism. Instead of being to the right of the domain—as is the case with Google links—the randomness for Grok Build links is positioned to the left of it. That allows the links to be easily enumerated using passive DNS services. These services monitor central DNS lookup servers. When a server lookup requests the IP address of a previously never-before-seen URL, the transaction is captured in a publicly searchable database. Had Grok followed Google’s approach, the links would have been invisible to passive DNS searchers. Muse, the Meta agent that CEO Mark Zuckerberg said was built from the ground up for security, recently suspended a link-sharing feature after it too was found leaking sensitive data.

In a recent development, aprozper said a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me. Of them, more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public, meaning that clicking on the link opened the corresponding app and all data it stored. He said that tests he conducted over the past week showed that, by default, Grok sets links to “Anyone with the link.” Users have the option to change the setting to “invited users” or “only you.”.

A representative with Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired, remarked in an email that Grok Build “apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it.” The representative said that competing coding agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt also give people the ability to generate shareable links.

It has been revealed that aprozper’s tests contradict the representative’s statement. In all cases, Grok Build required people to change anyone with the link to one of the other two options.

In a recent development, the Cursor statement regarding other AI coding platforms is correct. Aprozper noted that app builders, including Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, “also give each app its own web address, so the same DNS records expose them, too. However, Grok is where we found by far the most sensitive company data.” That means that people using these other platforms are also at risk of exposing sensitive data through shared links. Interestingly, AI platforms that follow the correct sharing link practice include Claude’s published artifacts (claude.ai/public/artifacts/), ChatGPT’s shared conversations (chatgpt.com/share/), and Gemini (gemini.google.com/share/). For all three, the secret randomness is in the path, so DNS never sees it.

Sources indicate that the representative didn’t respond to follow-up questions, including if SpaceXSI intentionally exposed the proprietary internal information, why the tech giant removed the data after Ars asked about it, and if it planned to notify customers who also exposed similar types of information. Anyone using shareable links with Grok Build should choose the “invite others” option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows users to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones. Text strings in Google’s SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a similar feature for compatible Android phones, according to Android Authority.

Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch. Little information is currently available about the feature’s limitations, including which phones or mobile carriers may not be compatible.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

On Apple’s side, any iPhone in the US running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM can use iPhone Handoff. AT&T does not right now support iPhone Handoff.

However, the code strings uncovered by Android Authority show that Android’s Fast Switch will work similarly to iPhone Handoff, in that users must be signed in to both devices under the same Google account for the feature to work.

Strings in Google’s SIM Manager app also point to no sharing between two customers, so this feature isn’t a way to circumvent carrier fees by adding service to someone else’s phone for the price of one.

If Fast Switch works anything like iPhone Handoff, which it appears it will, one eSIM can be switched between two phones. So, calls, messages, location services, and other information synced to your Apple ID can remain consistent between two devices.

Also: 5 hidden iOS 27 features that make older iPhones better.

Some third-party apps, like banking, communications, or social media, may also remain consistent across the two phones, depending on the app’s syncing behavior.

Sources indicate that features like Apple’s iPhone Handoff and Google’s Fast Switch are ideal for people who regularly use two phones. Business owners and digital creators may want one phone strictly for business purposes and the other for personal use.

Also: Google Wallet turns your Android phone into a digital house key.

According to recent reports, in that case, one person can keep up with two phones without paying for two phone service lines through their carrier. Still, customers will incur a fee, as T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month.

According to recent reports, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a great pick for smartwatch owners on a budget, and with this Black Friday offer at T-Mobile, you can get one on your wrist for free right now. Simply adding a fresh line on the carrier’s Watch Blueprint Plus will save you $300, which covers the full cost of the basic 40mm model.

Industry observers note that just note that there are a couple of conditions for this deal. The savings will be applied as bill credits over 36 months, so you’ll have to stay with T-Mobile for the full three years to get the watch paid in full. If you want to cancel service before then, you’ll be on the hook for the remaining value.

In a recent development, additionally, you’ll also pay the $35 connection charge up front. And if you want a larger display, this offer is also available for the 44mm model. You’re still saving $300, which knocks the cost down to less than $1 per month.

In a recent development, the Watch SE 3 is the most affordable wearable in Apple’s lineup, and it has plenty to offer, particularly if you’re looking for a basic smartwatch that works well. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices.
  • According to recent reports, the Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10.
  • Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor strategy of the customer’s home or business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the firm’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.

According to recent reports, the Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to blueprint patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.

Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor strategy of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.

However, flying and roving cameras with AI-enabled features could introduce new privacy risks for homes and businesses, on top of existing concerns involving fixed Ring cameras installed in room corners or as doorbell cameras.

Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the company’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.

But the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.

In a recent development, onboard camera capability includes a 148-degree field of view and 360-degree rotation with a 2K video resolution. Two LED lights also activate in low-light conditions to help illuminate the scene for the drone video camera.

However, the drone is limited to just 8 minutes of flight time when operating on a “latest, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions” according to the product description. It comes with a docking station for charging.

Another caveat in the product description is that the Ring Drone Cam may experience degraded performance when navigating in environments with reflective surfaces such as “polished marble or wet tile,” blank matte walls without any features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.

It has been revealed that still, Amazon touts the drone as providing an “autonomous way to check on your home that has never existed before,” whether the customer is away or at home. The Ring Drone can be controlled directly from the Alexa Home Map interactive map that highlights all of a customer’s Amazon-linked devices.

Meanwhile, Amazon has pitched the Ring Rover Cam priced at $1,000 as “an autonomous security robot designed for business.” This product is already available for preorder for those so inclined and scheduled to start shipping to customers on December 16, 2026.

The firm described the Ring Rover as being inspired by customer feedback involving another invite-only beta product, the Amazon Astro robot designed for home monitoring.

According to recent reports, the Ring Rover can livestream and record in up to 4K video resolution when patrolling or while doing a 360-degree scan at a designated location. Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and “Live View” events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.

Like the Ring Drone, the Ring Rover can automatically respond to alerts from connected Ring devices by following its preprogrammed patrol points. But the wheeled robot is only designed to operate within a single-floor, indoor environment because it lacks stair-climbing capability.

Amazon’s product description also warns that the Rover is not compatible with “curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.”.

To help compensate for its ground-based view, the Ring Rover comes with an automatically adjustable mast to peer over counters, shelving and other obstacles. It can supposedly cover up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters), according to Amazon’s product description.

The Ring Rover also comes with additional security-related features such as a siren and light tower to loudly announce its presence, along with a microphone for two-way audio communication if the customer wants to address someone near the robot.

Industry observers note that amazon touts the upcoming Ring Robotics products as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” with features such as LED indicators and screen notifications informing customers when video and audio recordings are active. But Ring, as an Amazon subsidiary, has been previously implicated in multiple privacy and security scandals.

Sources indicate that ring was previously charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch Ring video recordings of customers’ private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having lackluster safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts.

In a recent development, videos taken by the new Ring Drone and Ring Rover will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption that was introduced in September 2026, according to Amazon’s announcement. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has described this as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings, but still well short of end-to-end encryption.

The EFF has also called out what it describes as Ring founder Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach to Ring devices, including Ring reintroducing features that allow law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access from Ring people’ home security devices.

According to recent reports, amazon’s previous attempt to launch its Ring Always Home Cam drone also led to expanded privacy concerns. Ryan Calo, a law and technology researcher at the University of Washington, previously described such a flying security camera as providing upcoming ways to surveil others indoors, along with giving companies much greater access to potentially sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.

There is currently no mention of the latest Ring Robotics products implementing facial recognition or similar AI-powered technologies for identifying people. But starting in December 2025, Ring has allowed owners of fixed Ring doorbell cameras to turn on a “Familiar Faces” feature that uses facial recognition technology on visitors—and that is already the subject of a class action lawsuit.

Morning Minute: The CFTC Officially Greenlights Perps in the US, Starting with Backpack

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • 🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals.
  • For years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals.

For years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch. On Monday, that officially changed.

Chairman Michael Selig approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to run regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that execute and settle on blockchain rails. Selig called it “an crucial milestone in the evolution of American financial markets.”.

Backpack got both pieces at once, a Designated Contract Market designation to run the exchange and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration to clear its own trades. It intends to offer Americans round-the-clock leveraged crypto perps on a single global order book, accepting both fiat and crypto as collateral with cross-margin across positions. tZERO received its exchange approval a week earlier, after already holding clearing registration, and is building it into a derivatives vertical inside its infrastructure business.

Backpack US president Mark Wetjen, himself a former CFTC commissioner, framed it as “moving price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.” CEO Armani Ferrante noted the firm enters markets “fully regulated from day one.” Backpack already runs licensed platforms in Europe, Asia and the UAE.

The CFTC has certainly been busy this month. They cleared single-stock perpetual futures on November 3. It issued guidance on November 5 telling federally regulated exchanges they generally cannot restrict access by state. Now it has approved blockchain-native exchanges and clearinghouses.

Selig is building an onshore home for every product the offshore venues were built to serve, and he is doing it through staff action rather than legislation, with one sitting commissioner and nomination hearings for two more this week.

Industry observers note that hyperliquid is the obvious candidate and also the one that has publicly said it doesn’t want this. Jeff Yan spent his Bloomberg interview this month arguing Hyperliquid is infrastructure rather than an exchange, and that regulators should oversee the firms deploying markets on top rather than the chain underneath. His US route is HIP-3 partners taking on the compliance burden, with ICE investing in Trade.xyz and Kraken’s parent reportedly in talks. Backpack getting a DCM and a DCO makes that argument harder, because it demonstrates a crypto-native venue can simply register.

Then there’s Lighter. It has run Robinhood Wallet’s perps since July on a dedicated instance with a 50/50 revenue split, which is the partner model rather than the registration model. The registered model opens up with a CFTC license, and many think Lighter could very well be next.

One thing’s certain—the CFTC is serious about bringing perps onshore. From Selig himself, “I look forward to building on that milestone.” And we will find out soon enough who’s next….

The Aura brings the full Android XR ecosystem to customers via the connected Puck for a starting price of $1,099, while also functioning as standard XR glasses. For context, this is some serious value, especially since Samsung’s Galaxy XR starts at $1,799.

When I first opened the Xreal Aura, I thought it was another pair of the Xreal 1 Pro Plus. The hardware is nearly identical, except for two small cameras in the top corners of the front of the glasses to capture gestures. There is also a center-mounted camera similar to the Eye found on the Xreal Pro series, for capturing content and 6DoF spatial anchoring. Despite the additional cameras, the glasses still weigh only 95 grams — far less than the Samsung Galaxy XR’s 545 grams.

Industry observers note that speaking of gestures, I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive they were. With the Samsung Galaxy XR, I became frustrated quickly with gesture navigation and ended up using a connected Bluetooth mouse. Here, they’re much more usable.

There are physical buttons for control as well. The right arm has three: a small button at the top, one at the bottom, and a longer button behind it, primarily used for volume control. With the Puck connected, the buttons provide basic controls for volume, transparency level, and recentering the display. Audio comes through the slot speakers near the arms of the glasses and sounds great with minimal leakage thanks to the glasses’ partnership with Bose.

The guts of Android XR are contained in the puck that connects to the glasses. It’s about the size of a standard smartphone, but without a display. The top serves as a touchpad for navigation and menu selections in Android XR, if you prefer that method over gestures. The power button doubles as a fingerprint sensor to secure the Puck and unlock it with a simple tap. The longer volume button is just below the power button.

Sources indicate that there are two USB-C ports on the bottom: the left is for charging (mostly), and the right is to connect your Xreal glasses. You can also charge the Puck while using it, so if you are on a long flight, you can connect it to the glasses. The Xreal Aura Puck has a decent advertised battery life of 4-5 hours, compared to Apple Vision Pro and Samsung’s Galaxy XR at up to 2.5 hours.

In a recent development, the Xreal Aura is the first Android XR device to launch with a sleek glasses form factor — exactly what I wanted to see to improve the VR/AR experience for the end user. By contrast, the heavy Apple Vision Pro and Galaxy XR remain fairly niche due to their high prices and very large size.

Android XR brings the full Android experience to the glasses, with up to five displays you can move around in the virtual space, immersive experiences that can take you to other worlds or deep below the ocean surface, and optimal productivity options powered by thousands of Android apps.

Also: I compared the 3 best XR display glasses right now – the winner was not the most expensive.

With the Puck’s lightweight form factor and belt clip, you can walk around and quickly switch to Follow mode to see the world around you through the glasses, with your Android XR content positioned in a small window off to the side. Just tap the Follow mode button again to return to the full Android XR environment.

It has been revealed that one rather unique option I was unaware of until I read through the manual was the option to connect an external source to the USB-C charge port for a hybrid experience. Xreal calls this mode Wired Mirroring, and includes a shortcut to enable it in the Android XR launcher.

Plugging into a laptop brings your PC or Mac’s display to the glasses, giving the option to mirror or extend from your connected computer and then take full advantage of increasing the size of the display, moving in closer or further away from you, and viewing up to four other Android apps within the Android XR user interface.

I enjoy using this mode when I have something up on my computer to work on, with another piece of content streaming or another app open to gather data from in Android XR. I admit, it’ll take some time for me to get used to this unique mode, but it seems it can increase productivity, especially with the ability to peek below the lenses and see the other display on my computer.

Previously, devices like a Nintendo Switch 2 couldn’t connect to a pair of smart glasses because they’re designed to output video only via a dock. The Xreal Puck functions similarly to the Xreal AR adapter, so it “fools” the Switch 2 into thinking it is docked, then outputs the game video to the Xreal Aura glasses. You don’t need the Xreal AR adapter, as the Puck now serves this role and has its own power, eliminating the need for a USB-C power source.

Since the Xreal Aura glasses looked so much like the Xreal 1 Pro Plus I recently tested, I decided to plug my Apple iPhone Duo into the Xreal Aura, and voila! They performed just like the 1 Pro Plus, including the full on-screen display menu options. I later read in the manual that this is called external display mode.

Also: I invested in Samsung’s $1,800 XR headset to replace my dual monitors – and it’s paying off big time.

While you should not purchase the Xreal Aura solely to serve as standard XR glasses, it is fantastic to have this option, since there are times when you may want to use the glasses without the Android XR platform. For example, when I travel for work with just a Surface Pro, I want a substantial ultra-wide screen experience directly from the Surface Pro to the glasses. This lets me travel with just the Xreal Aura and promptly switch to the Android XR experience for other tasks.

Recent findings suggest that apple TV and Netflix are right now unavailable on the Xreal Aura in Android XR, but you can watch them by plugging in your iPhone or Android directly into the glasses without using the Puck. This is why Xreal provides the ultimate flexibility with the Aura at a reasonable price point.

Xreal also sent along the Xreal Game Controller, co-branded with GameSir, as well as the Xreal Keyboard. The Game Controller has a charging stand that plugs into USB-C to charge the controller for hours of gameplay. Since I primarily game with a Nintendo Switch 2, I took off the removable magnet faceplate and swapped out the left directional pad for one that mimics the Switch 2.

After connecting via Bluetooth, I enjoyed an optimal gaming experience on my Switch 2 and the Xreal Aura. Even better, I activated Google Gemini directly from the controller to ask for help when stuck in game areas. As a casual gamer, this dual functionality motivated me to play more games.

Extensive text input is painful to do with just gestures, but voice-to-text is very accurate and fast. However, if you enjoy typing on a keyboard, you either need to connect a computer and use that keyboard while looking under the glasses, or connect a Bluetooth keyboard for mobile computing. The Xreal Keyboard has great key sizing and spacing, along with solid tactile feedback. It would be nice to have a trackpad attached, but finger gestures are fine too if a Bluetooth mouse is not connected to the Aura.

Also: I wear XR glasses every day on my commute – Why Xreal’s latest pair is my new main driver.

The Xreal Game Controller is available for $99 and the Xreal keyboard is $79, but there are frequently bundle offers that offer discounts.

Xreal provides exactly what I was hoping to see with Android XR with the new Xreal Aura glasses. They have a sleek form factor and offer the full package with a very nice carrying case. The 70-degree FOV is not as expansive as that of full-on heavy headsets, but it still provides an immersive experience that is sure to satisfy most people.

It has been revealed that the additional modes make the Aura an even better value, and it’s clear that this is the Android XR solution you want for maximum flexibility and productivity. I look forward to commuting, traveling, and working in a big-screen environment with this pair of glasses.

#2876. Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (711 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
  • Sources indicate that conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways.
  • According to recent reports, more broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Sources indicate that conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a fresh AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

According to recent reports, more broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn’t have critical vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind’s Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It has been revealed that the DeepMind analysis did not find any upcoming vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and indicated that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

According to recent reports, “While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind’s approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal’s chief technology officer, indicates in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code’s privacy guarantees.”.

It has been revealed that for critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” says Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind’s vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’”.

In a recent development, the open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has aims to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written,” Chaudhuri states. “There’s a middle ground.”.

Apple reveals daily limits on your Siri AI use – here’s how much you’ll have to pay

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that have you been using the new Siri AI?
  • Also: 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers.
  • Apple hasn’t been shy about stating that the use of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence for specific tasks would face daily access limits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that have you been using the new Siri AI? If so, how much? I’ve been turning to it a lot since the release of iOS 27. Well, how we use it — and how often — will soon depend on how much we pay for an iCloud+ plan.

Also: 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers.

Apple hasn’t been shy about stating that the use of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence for specific tasks would face daily access limits. Increased limits would be granted based on your iCloud+ subscription. Now the company has revealed how much it will cost you and when the limits will begin.

Recent findings suggest that “Starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for people with a supported device set to a supported language,” Apple said on a support page updated November 16. “Some features rely on powerful server models and have limits where increased access is available with eligible iCloud+ aims, starting with the 27.3 release.”.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in early December, so that’s when the daily usage limits will kick in.

At that point, people with no paid iCloud+ plan and even those with the $0.99-per-month 50 GB plan will be the most limited, with Apple saying only that they’ll face a “Standard Device Limit.”.

What is a standard limit? That depends not just on how many times you tap into Siri per day but on what tasks you assign it. Basic Siri commands, such as setting timers and alarms or sending standard text messages, will remain free and unlimited.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster.

Industry observers note that advanced Siri and Apple Intelligence tasks will bump into the usage limits. These include the following, according to Apple:.

One positive here is that the limits are per device not per account. That means you can use Siri AI and Apple Intelligence with the same account across your iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro without fear of chewing up too much of your quota.

Industry observers note that this all sounds like a way for Apple to steer people to more expensive iCloud+ accounts. But the limits are in place for a key reason. Basic commands are processed on your device, so they don’t require the use of Apple servers. More advanced tasks are processed using server-side AI models, which can feel the strain if too many people access them all at once.

Also: What you’ll pay for AI agents will be wildly variable and unpredictable.

Sources indicate that how will you know if you use up your daily allotment and what happens then? You’ll receive a notification if you hit your limit for a particular feature category. At that point, you can still give Siri basic tasks to perform. But advanced ones will be paused until your limit resets the next day. Otherwise, Apple is undoubtedly hoping that people who continually run into limits will upgrade to a pricier iCloud+ blueprint.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players.
  • Sources indicate that this particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the concern in private discussion groups.
  • Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they remarked, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Major Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.

Sources indicate that this particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the concern in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”.

Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they remarked, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.

The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”.

Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Substantial Walk‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”.

Sources indicate that that limited AI use—which House House indicates represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House said it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game (At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).

House House mentioned it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Substantial Walk‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”.

The IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House said.

Sources indicate that “This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Substantial Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”.

Learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Significant Walk. In a blog post discussing his feelings, IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”.

But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who remarked that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.

“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”.

This isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).

“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they noted at the time.

Since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Massive Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.

But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s important to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.

IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”.

“To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.

Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He stated he considers Massive Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”.

In a recent development, “They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added. “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”.

Industry observers note that but some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog.

Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”.

As time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines, it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). That noted, many still see value in a firm and unyielding public stance against what they see as a scourge to their entire industry.

“I think zero tolerance is a viable political position,” narrative designer and writer Hannah Nicklin wrote on social media. “You use politics against systems, for people you affect change through connection and understanding… The IGF jury statement… levels itself at a system of shared value and asks for change to enable solidarity around a position of harm reduction.”.

#2867. This power bank lets me send texts without cell service or Wi-Fi – here’s how

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (883 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

This power bank lets me send texts without cell service or Wi-Fi – here’s how

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve covered a lot of power banks, from ones that are thinner than your phone to huge ones that can power laptops.
  • Also: Stop putting your phone in rice – I can confirm this Dryout bag works better.
  • In a recent development, yes, that’s right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve covered a lot of power banks, from ones that are thinner than your phone to huge ones that can power laptops. But I can say — hand on heart — that I’ve never seen a power bank that can connect to a decentralized communication network.

Also: Stop putting your phone in rice – I can confirm this Dryout bag works better.

In a recent development, yes, that’s right. When push comes to shove, and the lights go out or there’s no cell tower for miles, this power bank can take over from your phone if the network goes down and keep you connected. This is the Heltec Automation 5,000mAh power bank.

Looking at this from the perspective of a power bank, it’s a 5,000mAh unit with a 15W Qi2 wireless charging pad on the front and an input/output USB-C port on the bottom delivering up to 20W.

And yes, all the ports do what it says on the box they’ll do. It measures 3.9 x 2.9 x 0.4 inches and weighs a hair under 5 ounces. There are three buttons on the power bank; one is the usual power button (marked USER on this unit), and the other two are to do with the communication feature built into the unit.

Also, on the side is a magnetic pogo-pin connector that I initially thought was the charging port, but it’s thankfully only needed to flash new firmware onto the device.

There’s also a very neat 2.13-inch E Ink display that’s perfect because not only is it totally readable under the brightest sunlight, but it also uses very little power, drawing on the battery only when the screen updates.

The E Ink display is used in combination with the buttons marked USR and RST to control the unit.

Looking at this as a power bank, it’s a small but decent unit, but if it is just portability you’re after, you’ll have no problems finding a smaller, lighter device. It’s not exactly the thinnest around, but that’s because other power banks don’t have built-in comms.

OK, time to talk about the comms. This is no ordinary walkie-talkie or cell phone in disguise. It uses a system called Meshtastic, which is like combining a walkie-talkie with SMS.

The idea is that you use Bluetooth to pair the unit with a smartphone (some Meshtastic devices have a built-in keyboard, so you don’t need to do this, but this one needs a smartphone), and you use the Meshtastic app to send short text messages to other users.

The radio uses LoRa, a long-range, low-power technology designed to transmit small amounts of data over long distances. And that data is text only. No voice, no photos, no internet access. And by short, I’m talking about a couple of hundred characters.

How far? As with most things, it depends, and you’ll come across some absolutely outrageous claims online. Yes, the ground-to-ground record is 205 miles, but a typical user is going to get anywhere from a few hundred yards to up to about a mile in a town or among trees, or about 3 to 6 miles over open ground.

Also: LaCie’s 256TB DAS is a beast, but I only recommend it to one kind of user.

Industry observers note that but Meshtastic has a trick up its sleeve, and the clue is in the name: mesh. Each Meshtastic device is its own node, and most nodes help pass on — or relay — messages by default, boosting the range of an individual radio. So, the effectiveness of Meshtastic relies on having plenty of users with devices, as well as others putting up permanent router nodes on rooftops and hilltops to help to boost Meshtastic transmission ranges for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not going to bog you down with all the details, but if you want to dive down that rabbit hole, the Meshtastic website is the best place to start. But let me warn you, it’s a deep one!

A magnetic power bank is the perfect form factor for a Meshtastic device because it needs power, and, as I stated earlier, you need a smartphone to create your messages and send them via Bluetooth to the Meshtastic radio for beaming out into the world.

So, it’s always attached to your phone and ready. And if you’re worried about the wireless charging pad draining the battery, a double-press of the CTRL button turns that off. Battery life when running the Meshtastic radio is excellent, easily good for a few days between recharges.

Not everyone needs a Meshtastic power bank (heck, most people won’t even know what Meshtastic is, or that this technology exists). But I see this catching the eye of two types of people — outdoor enthusiasts looking for a decentralized comms system that doesn’t rely on any infrastructure outside their control, and those who want a radio-based hobby but don’t want to mess about with the FCC or get any licenses.

And for $69, this Heltec Automation Meshtastic power bank a cheap way to get into the Meshtastic world — you might get hooked, and before you know it, you’ll be putting up solar-powered relay nodes and telling everyone they need to get into LoRa radio too.
